item.title: Atlantic Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
000
ABNT20 KNHC 212316
TWOAT

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 PM EDT Wed Oct 21 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on newly formed
Subtropical Storm Josephine, located a few hundred miles offshore
of the United States Mid-Atlantic coast.

Subtropical Central Atlantic:
A trough of low pressure located several hundred miles to the
east-southeast of Bermuda is producing a large area of disorganized
showers and thunderstorms. Some development of this system is
possible during the next day or two while it moves slowly
north-northeastward. Upper-level winds are forecast to become too
strong for further development by the weekend.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...10 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...low...10 percent.

&&
Public Advisories on Josephine are issued under WMO header WTNT35
KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCPAT5.
Forecast/Advisories on Josephine are issued under WMO header WTNT25
KNHC and under AWIPS header MIATCMAT5.

$$
Forecaster Reinhart

item.title: Subtropical Storm Josephine Public Advisory Number 2
item.description:
Issued at 1100 PM AST Wed Oct 21 2026 
000
WTNT35 KNHC 220254
TCPAT5
 
BULLETIN
Subtropical Storm Josephine Advisory Number   2
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL102026
1100 PM AST Wed Oct 21 2026
 
...JOSEPHINE EXPECTED TO MOVE NORTHEASTWARD AWAY FROM THE UNITED
STATES ON THURSDAY...
...FORECAST TO BECOME A POWERFUL EXTRATROPICAL CYCLONE...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 1100 PM AST...0300 UTC...INFORMATION
-----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...37.7N 69.4W
ABOUT 245 MI...390 KM S OF NANTUCKET MASSACHUSETTS
ABOUT 565 MI...905 KM SW OF HALIFAX NOVA SCOTIA
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...65 MPH...100 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...NNE OR 15 DEGREES AT 6 MPH...9 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...988 MB...29.18 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 1100 PM AST (0300 UTC), the center of Subtropical Storm Josephine 
was located near latitude 37.7 North, longitude 69.4 West. The storm 
is moving toward the north-northeast near 6 mph (9 km/h). A turn 
toward the northeast with an increase in forward speed is expected 
tomorrow, followed by an eastward motion on Friday and into the 
weekend. On the forecast track, Josephine should move away from the 
United States and remain south of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland 
during the next couple of days.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 65 mph (100 km/h) with higher 
gusts. Some strengthening is forecast while Josephine remains a 
subtropical storm through early Thursday. Further strengthening is 
likely later on Thursday, and Josephine could become a post-tropical 
cyclone with hurricane-force winds.
 
Winds of 40 mph extend outward up to 415 miles (665 km) from the
center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 988 mb (29.18 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
WIND: Gale-force winds are possible in gusts along portions of the
northeastern United States coast through Thursday. See products
issued by your local National Weather Service office for more
details.
 
COASTAL FLOODING: Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding is
ongoing along portions of the U.S. Mid-Atlantic coast and will
continue through the rest of the week around times of high tide.
Please refer to products issued by your local National Weather
Service forecast office for more information.
 
SURF: Large swells generated by Josephine are affecting much of the
eastern seaboard of the United States and portions of Atlantic
Canada. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and
rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local
weather office.
 
A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found
at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at5.shtml?ripCurrents
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 500 AM AST.
 
$$
Forecaster Reinhart

item.title: Subtropical Storm Josephine Forecast Discussion Number 1
item.description:
Issued at 500 PM AST Wed Oct 21 2026 
000
WTNT45 KNHC 212047
TCDAT5
 
Subtropical Storm Josephine Discussion Number   1
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL102026
500 PM AST Wed Oct 21 2026

The non-tropical area of low pressure (Invest AL93) that we have 
been monitoring this week has acquired enough subtropical 
characteristics to be considered a subtropical storm.  
Scatterometer data showed that fronts near the cyclone had 
dissipated, with a smaller radius-of-maximum wind than yesterday.  
Additionally moderate-to-deep convection has been organizing near 
and west of the warm-core center.  Thus, advisories have been 
initiated on a subtropical storm, and 55 kt is shown as the initial 
intensity based on the scatterometer data.

Josephine has been moving slowly northward today as a shortwave 
ridge passes across the northeastern United States.  The storm 
should accelerate northeastward tomorrow as a mid-latitude trough 
digs into the Great Lakes and Northeastern United States, taking 
the system away from the US.  By Friday, the low should turn 
eastward, to the south of Newfoundland.  Model guidance is in good 
agreement on this path, and the new forecast is close to a blend of 
the global model consensus and the NOAA corrected-consensus aid 
HCCA.

The subtropical storm will likely intensify during the next day or 
so through a favorable trough interaction while it remains near the 
north wall of the Gulf Stream.  Global models are in good agreement 
on a band of hurricane-force winds developing tomorrow on the back 
side of the low as it undergoes extratropical transition.  A slow 
weakening is anticipated by late Friday with the loss of forcing 
from the trough while the system moves over cold water.  The NHC 
intensity forecast is similar to a blend of the GFS/ECMWF global 
model solutions.  The cyclone should become absorbed in about 4 
days within a much larger low over the North Atlantic.  

Since the coastal wind hazards with this system have been covered 
for the last several days through non-tropical products issued by 
local National Weather Service offices, and the system is forecast 
to move away from the coast, those products will remain in effect 
until the threat diminishes.
